content.title: I played for Iowa coach Ben McCollum. These 3 words define him
content.text: This story is part of Peak, The Athletic’s desk covering the mental side of sports. Sign up for Peak’s newsletter here.Ryan Hawkins played for Iowa coach Ben McCollum for five seasons at Northwest Missouri State. McCollum won four NCAA Division II titles at Northwest Missouri, spent one season at Drake and was hired at Iowa before this season. No. 9 seed Iowa defeated No. 4 seed Nebraska on Thursday in the Sweet 16. The whole embodiment of Ben McCollum comes down to one saying: Impose your will.Every season I played for him at Northwest Missouri State, he handed out binders to every player. Those words were always on the cover page.Coach McCollum wanted us to dictate how the game was played. He wanted us to impose our will on offense by taking the shots we wanted. He wanted us to play at our own pace. The mindset filtered down to every part of the program. When we went through preseason conditioning, he wanted us to impose our will on the workout.Don’t put your hands on your knees, he said.That was the workout imposing its will on you.If you need help, put it around your teammate’s shoulders.Your browser does not support the video tag.Everyone had the ultimate trust in him because you knew he was going to identify your strengths. I redshirted my first year at Northwest Missouri. Coach once called me “a deer on ice.” I was a stretch four who still needed to develop my shot. But I think I fit the stereotype of the kind of player he wanted: tough guys who were going to play hard and give maximum effort.And once he identified what you were great at, he wanted you to do it constantly. He never said: Don’t do this. He always said: You do this really well. So let’s do this as much as possible.His approach was so unique. He was so locked in on details like the angles of screens and the timing of back cuts. He always wanted to run actions that played toward people’s strengths.Every day in practice, we would have a period where we played half-court, five-on-five, and he would just tinker with sets and plays that we already used, just to get different looks.We used to run “Spanish action” — a pick-and-roll set with a back screen for the screener. It was a simple set, but it fit my game perfectly. So we ran it a lot.Coach McCollum once told us about the book “Good to Great” by Jim Collins. It’s about why some businesses thrive and others don’t. But it encapsulated the kind of offense he wanted. If you could get two feet in the paint, you might have a good shot. But somebody outside on the perimeter is probably going to have a great shot. He wanted us to create good shots, then take great shots. It was all about building a culture of serving others.He hated what he called “energy vampires,” a phrase he borrowed from another book, “The Energy Bus.” He didn’t like moody players. If we didn’t have a good attitude, he would send us back to the locker room and then have us come back. He valued consistency and held everyone to a standard. The first day of practice, he always set the standard with intensity, and the coaching staff was always just as energetic and passionate.I used to get out of class and the staff would be playing “noon ball” — a pickup run in the middle of the day. Coach always got after it. He wasn’t a great shooter, but he was always getting into the lane and finding the open guy.He played relentless defense and took it personally if he lost. To this day, I think he still knows his noon ball record.The other part was his loyalty. He showed it to guys who were in the program for two, three, four years, and you could see the progress guys made.On my second day on campus at Northwest Missouri, I played with the guys for the first time. I remember thinking: I’m not cut out for this. If you watched me play as a freshman, there’s no way you would have thought I’d ever play beyond college. All these years later, I’m playing professional basketball in Germany.It goes back to the trust. He was able to get us to put our heart and our minds into the development. He could identify your talents and hide your weaknesses.If you were fortunate enough to be coached by him, you understood the detail and preparation and effort that he put into every game. The success was going to come just because of how determined he was.Last weekend, I watched No. 9 Iowa beat No. 1 seed Florida in the second round of the NCAA Tournament. It was a perfect embodiment of Coach. They slowed the pace. And they imposed their will.— As told to Rustin Dodd
